markdown.markdown:
- Many modern scientific problems/tasks are too larger or too complex (or both) to *solve* without the aid of computers - some problems are hard to even visualize/imagine without computers

- Programming is the act of providing computers with specific operational instructions; usually to assist (us) with performing a specific task or solving a specific problem

- Can provide instructions via mouse and keyboard (i.e., use a software tool); but the majority of programming (coding) is done through written instructions called **source code** ## Basics of programming - the programming *language* used to write source code depends on: - the hardware/software of the computer (or instrument) - i.e., what can the computer process/understand - the task/problem being worked on - the skills/experience of the programmer

## Basics of programming - one major dichotomy to know: - **Compiled Languages:** source code gets compiled by an *operating system specific compiler* into an **executable file** (application) that can then be run directly by the operating system - language has a steeper learning curve, but the resulting applications run very efficiently

- **Interpreted Languages:** source code is executed by an interpreter (application) which being run on the operating system - language is more human-readable, but usually inefficient

- In this class we'll be working with the R programming language ## Programming in R - To write R code, all you need is to know the language!

- To *run* R code, all you need to have is: - A computer with any modern operating system (Windows, Max, Linux) - A text editor installed on the computer - The appropriate version of "R" (the interpreter) installed on the computer [www.cran.r-project.org](www.cran.r-project.org){target="_blank"}

- [RStudio](www.https://posit.co/products/open-source/rstudio){target="_blank"} is an integrated development environment (IDE) application - allows you to view/edit code, run the code, visualize outputs in a console, and view all the variables currently loaded in the interpreting environment ## Errors - syntax are the set of rules/procedures for working with a language (grammarPlus) - compilers/interpreters are very sensitive to syntax--you need to follow the rules of your language for your code to run (syntax errors)

- compilers/interpreters are more literal than humans - you need to make sure your logic is precise for your code to output the correct answer (logic errors)

- if your computer is not following the instructions you've provided, there is either a syntax error, a logic error, or a memory leak ## Some key R syntax ::: {.fragment} ```{r} # # ignores text that follows until the next line (comment) x <- 7 # create a variable x and assign it the value 7 y = 8 # create a variable y and assign it the value 8 z = x + y # create a variable z and assign it the value of x + y zebra = x^2 # create a variable zebra and assigned the value of x to the power 2 ``` :::
:::{.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false print(zebra) # the function "print" displays the value of zebra maintaining its "shape" ``` :::
:::{.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false ebra = zebra - z # creates a variable ebra and assign it the value of zebra - z cat(ebra) # the function "cat" displays the value of variable ebra ``` :::
:::{.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false cat(zebra - z) # the function "cat" displays the value of variable zebra - z ``` ::: ## Some key R syntax :::{.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false cat("This is a test") # display the string "This is a test" # cat(test) # this code will fail because there is no variable named test in our environment ``` :::
:::{.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false zebra_sentence = paste0("The value of zebra is ",zebra) # The paste0 function will glue things together without including any spaces cat(zebra_sentence) ``` :::
:::{.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false cat(paste0("The value of ebra is ",ebra) ) ``` ::: ## Objects in R - Some key types of objects to be aware of: - variable: stores a single value, can be a number or character - array: stores multiple values, can contain numbers XOR characters (vectors + matrices) - data frames: multiple arrays, can be any data type but will force a "shape" on the data - lists: multiple variables, arrays, etc.. can be any data type AND any shape ::: {.fragment} ```{r} rm(list=ls()) # the ls() function finds all objects in the environment, the rm() function removes and lists that are provided to it x = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5) # creates an array x and assigns it the values 1 through 5 using the the "collect" function y = seq(1,5,1) # creates an array y and assigns it the values 1 through 5 increments of 1 using the "sequence" function z = seq(1,5,0.1) # creates an array z and assigns it the values 1 through 5 by increments of 0.1 using the "sequence" ``` ::: ## Objects in R ::: {.fragment} ```{r} xy = cbind(x,y) # use the "cbind" function create a matrix xy with columns equal to x and y print(xy) ``` :::
::: {.fragment} ```{r} cat(xy) ``` ::: ## Importing data in R - R is a general purpose programming language, but it is popular because of its rich repository of powerful statistics and data analysis functions - Reading and writing data - Regression modeling - Hypothesis testing - Machine learning ::: {.fragment} ```{r} rm(list=ls()) # clear work space Spec1 = read.table("U1.txt") # create an array Spec1 and assign it the values from the text file U1.txt using the read.table function # the first column is m/z values and second column are intensity values nPeaks = nrow(Spec1) # create a variable nPeaks and assign it the value of the number of rows in the array Spec1 using the nrow function nPeaks # instead of using the print or cat function, in the console we can just type the variable name and its value will get printed on the screen ``` ::: ## Work with mass spectral data ::: {.fragment} ```{r} plot(Spec1) # use the plot function to create a scatter plot of the x,y value in Spec1 ``` ::: [**Issues:** atypical for plotting mass spectra (raw abundance scores, and scatter plot)]{.fragment} ## Work with mass spectral data ::: {.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false mz = Spec1[,1] # with an array, we can extract specific columns, rows and cell values int = Spec1[,2] int = int/max(int) # normalizes the intensity values to 1 plot(mz, int, type="h", xlab="mass-to-charge ratio", ylab="relative intensity") # use the plot function to create a scatter plot of the x,y value in Spec1 ``` :::
[**Issues:** a lot of low intensity peaks that could be artifacts]{.fragment} ## Work with mass spectral data ::: {.fragment} ```{r} #| output: false noisePeaks = which(int<=0.01) # identify the values in the intensity array that have relative intensity less than 1% if(length(noisePeaks)>0){ # checks to see if any noise peaks were identified, if yes runs code in the "chunck" mz = mz[-noisePeaks] int = int[-noisePeaks] } plot(mz, int, type="h", xlab="mass-to-charge ratio", ylab="relative intensity") # use the plot function to create a scatter plot of the x,y value in Spec1 ``` :::
[**Homework challenge:** write some code to determine the mass-to-charge ratio of the base peak of this spectrum]{.fragment} ## Working in the console versus writing a script - Why write and save scripts? - allows you to easily update and re-run your source code - allows you to share your source code with other people

- Why work in the console? - to test some ideas out or compute something quickly

- \>90% of the time, you'll want to write a script ## Coming up - Seminars are running in-person on Thursday October 15th
- F01 (SC 204) and F02 (SC W1)

- **SPECIAL Lecture next week:** Graduate school in Canada - Guests will be joining us via Zoom
